title: Organise and carry out game capture and removal operations

lessons.title: Why we capture and remove game, and how to plan it
lessons.html:
Game capture starts with the management plan

On a game farm, nature reserve or conservancy, animals are not captured on a whim. Every capture and removal operation must link back to the management plan for the area. The plan sets the carrying capacity of the veld, the target numbers per species, and the reasons for moving animals in or out.

Common reasons for capture and removal

  • Overstocking: veld condition assessments show that grazers such as blue wildebeest or zebra exceed what the camps can carry, especially before a dry winter.
  • Sales and income: live game sales to other properties or auctions bring in revenue (in ZAR) that funds the reserve.
  • Genetic management: bringing in new bloodlines or removing breeding males to avoid inbreeding.
  • Disease control and veterinary work: testing for diseases, treating injured animals, or meeting veterinary movement rules.
  • Reintroduction and range expansion: stocking a new reserve or returning a species to its historical range.
  • Damage control: removing animals that break fences or damage crops on neighbouring farms.

Planning the operation

As a supervisor you take part in the planning team with the reserve manager, the wildlife veterinarian and the capture contractor. A good plan answers these questions:

  1. Which animals and how many? Species, sex, age class and numbers, taken from the management plan or sale agreement.
  2. Which permits? Provincial conservation permits for capture and transport, and for threatened or protected species the permits under the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 (TOPS regulations). Veterinary movement rules may also apply.
  3. Which technique? Mass capture into a boma with a helicopter, drop nets, darting from a vehicle or helicopter, or passive capture with a capture boma at a water point.
  4. When? Cooler months and early mornings reduce heat stress. Avoid late pregnancy and the peak of the lambing or calving season.
  5. Who does what? Clear roles for the vet, pilot, boma team, crate team, drivers and data recorder.
  6. What can go wrong? Capture myopathy, injuries, escapes, vehicle breakdowns and veld fires. Each risk needs a plan.

Only a veterinarian, or a person authorised under the relevant law, may use immobilising drugs. Your team supports them; you never handle or dose these drugs yourself unless you are legally authorised and trained.

lessons.title: Executing the capture and removal safely
lessons.html:
On the day of capture

Start with a briefing before sunrise. Every person must know their role, the radio channels, the hand signals and the emergency plan. Check that the first aid kit, fire beaters, water, shade cloth and the vet's emergency kit are on site.

Mass capture with a boma

  • The boma is a funnel of opaque plastic or shade cloth curtains that leads into a dark holding pen and then into the loading ramp and truck or crates.
  • The helicopter herds animals slowly towards the funnel. Curtains are closed behind the group by the boma team, who stay hidden and quiet until the signal.
  • Keep chase distances and times as short as possible. Long chases cause capture myopathy, a muscle breakdown that can kill animals hours or days later.

Darting and chemical capture

  • The vet selects the drug and dose. The team keeps sight of the darted animal and approaches only on the vet's signal.
  • Once down, cover the eyes with a blindfold, keep the animal in a natural position on its chest where possible, and check breathing.
  • Keep people clear of the head and horns of species like kudu, gemsbok and buffalo.

Handling, loading and transport

  1. Work quietly. Noise and handling raise stress.
  2. Monitor temperature. If an animal is overheating, cool it with water and tell the vet immediately.
  3. Load animals into well ventilated, dark crates or a game truck with correct compartments. Do not mix species or horned males with females and young.
  4. Carry the permits and veterinary documents with the load.
  5. Drive smoothly and check the load at agreed stops.

Never

  • Never stand in front of a crate door or in the path of a running animal.
  • Never pick up a used dart or drug bottle. Some immobilising drugs are dangerous to humans in tiny amounts. Report it to the vet.
  • Never continue a chase that the vet or pilot has called off.

lessons.title: Samples, monitoring devices and the capture report
lessons.html:
Using the capture for science

A captured animal is a rare chance to collect information. The vet and ecologist will tell you which samples and data are needed, but the team helps collect, label and store them.

Typical samples and data

ItemPurpose
Blood samplesDisease testing, genetics, pregnancy
Hair or tissue (ear notch)DNA and parentage
Dung and ticksParasite loads
Body measurements and condition scoreHealth and growth records
Sex, age class, horn measurementsPopulation and trophy records

Label every tube with the animal ID, date, species and sample type. Keep blood samples cool and out of the sun. Record GPS position and time.

Fitting monitoring devices

Some animals are fitted with GPS or VHF collars, ear tags or microchips. Collars must fit snugly but leave room for neck growth and swelling; the vet or ecologist checks the fit. Record the collar serial number and frequency against the animal ID.

Preparing information for the report

After the operation, the organisation compiles a report for management, the buyer and the permit authority. Your job is to supply accurate information:

  • Number of animals captured per species, sex and age class.
  • Animals that died or were injured, with the cause as determined by the vet.
  • Samples taken and devices fitted.
  • Times, weather, technique used and problems encountered.
  • Permit numbers and destination of each load.

Write notes on the day; memory fades fast. Losses must be reported honestly, because they help improve the next operation.

Key points

  • Every capture must serve the area's management plan.
  • Permits and clear roles are arranged before the day.
  • Short chases, shade, quiet handling and cooling reduce capture myopathy.
  • Only vets or legally authorised people use immobilising drugs.
  • Label samples properly and record device numbers against animal IDs.
  • Accurate, honest records feed the operation report.
